evidence.claim: The East Steens Tour Route follows the mountain’s eastern escarpment and the Alvord Desert for 143 miles.
evidence.quote: This 143-mile tour skirts along the eastern escarpment of Steens Mountain and the vast expanses of the Alvord Desert

evidence.claim: Oregon DOT presents this Tour Route in its scenic-byways program as a study in contrasts, with five to seven hours of minimum driving time.
evidence.quote: Minimum Driving Time: 5-7 hours

evidence.claim: Part of the drive is gravel, with Steens Mountain to the west and desert salt flats to the east.
evidence.quote: Near milepost 65, the Tour Route detours off Highway 78 onto East Steens Road; it's a gravel surface, but quite passable for regular passenger vehicles.

evidence.claim: The highway portion acquired its number in 1932, when Oregon assigned Route 78 to the Burns-Crane Highway.
evidence.quote: OR 78 was assigned to the Burns-Crane Highway No. 24 when the Oregon route numbering system was initiated in 1932.

evidence.claim: Travel beside the Alvord once took a different course: in a 1977 oral history, George Renwick recalled drivers crossing the dry playa toward Mosquito Creek before a road was built along the basin’s edge.
evidence.quote: In a 1977 oral history, George Renwick recalled that drivers once crossed the dry playa toward Mosquito Creek before a road was built around the Alvord.

evidence.claim: The mountain-side stretch of East Steens Road is county-maintained gravel.
evidence.quote: A stretch of East Steens Road along the mountain side of the basin is a county-maintained gravel road.

evidence.claim: From Burns, take Route 78 southeast through Crane and New Princeton.
evidence.quote: OR 78 begins at an intersection with US 20 and US 395 in Burns and continues southeast through Crane and New Princeton to Burns Junction

evidence.claim: Near milepost 65, the tour turns onto East Steens Road.
evidence.quote: Near milepost 65, the Tour Route detours off Highway 78 onto East Steens Road

evidence.claim: The sagebrush-covered Sheepshead Mountains lie east of the road before a series of small lakes, which can be dry depending on the year.
evidence.quote: After passing the sagebrush-covered Sheepshead Mountains to the east, you come to a series of small lakes Five Cent, Ten Cent, Fifteen Cent and Juniper Lakes (the lakes can be dry depending on the year)

evidence.claim: Mann Lake comes next, then the Alvord salt flats, before the route ends at Fields.
evidence.quote: You'll next reach Mann Lake

evidence.quote: providing a scenic study in dramatic contrasts.

evidence.claim: Crane’s post office reopened when the Union Pacific Railroad arrived from Ontario in 1916.
evidence.quote: When the Union Pacific Railroad was completed from Ontario, Oregon, in 1916, the post office was reopened.

evidence.claim: Until the line reached Burns in 1924, the town was an important livestock shipping point, supporting four hotels, five restaurants and a dance hall.
evidence.quote: Until the railroad was finished to Burns in 1924, Crane was an important livestock shipping point, and the town was thriving with its five restaurants, four hotels, three garages, two general merchandise stores, a warehouse, a lumber yard, livery stables, a dance hall

evidence.claim: A series of fires, the last in 1938, preceded a lasting loss of prosperity.
evidence.quote: After a series of fires, the latest in 1938, however, the town never returned to its former prosperity.

evidence.claim: Crane Union High School serves a large rural district as a boarding school.
evidence.quote: The high school, which draws students from a large rural district, is a boarding school.

evidence.claim: The town takes its name from Crane Creek and Crane Creek Gap, a pass between the Harney Basin and the South Fork Malheur River’s drainage basin.
evidence.quote: Crane was named for the prominent local features Crane Creek and Crane Creek Gap. Crane Creek Gap is the pass between the Harney Basin and the drainage basin of the South Fork Malheur River.

evidence.claim: The Alvord’s salt surface records water arriving and disappearing.
evidence.quote: Streams flow onto the playa, but the basin has no outlet. The water evaporates, leaving salt minerals on the surface.

evidence.claim: Streams reach the playa at Steens Mountain’s eastern foot, but the basin has no outlet; evaporation leaves minerals behind.
evidence.quote: The Alvord Desert is a dry lake in Harney County, southeastern Oregon, at the eastern foot of Steens Mountain. The mountain rises more than a mile above the playa. Streams flow onto the playa, but the basin has no outlet. The water evaporates, leaving salt minerals on the surface.

evidence.claim: Faulting lowered the basin that holds this dry lake.
evidence.quote: Faulting lowered the basin that holds the Alvord playa.

evidence.claim: During the late Pleistocene, a much larger lake covered the playa, reaching more than 80 miles in length and up to 280 feet deep.
evidence.quote: During the late Pleistocene, a much larger lake covered the playa. At its highest level, it was more than 80 miles (130 km) long and up to 280 feet (85 m) deep.

evidence.claim: The playa can flood in wet periods, but it is dry for much of the year.
evidence.quote: The playa can flood in wet periods but is dry for much of the year.

evidence.claim: Salt minerals remain on the playa after water evaporates.
evidence.quote: The water evaporates, leaving salt minerals on the surface.

evidence.claim: Charles Fields settled here in 1881 and built a roadhouse serving the route between Winnemucca and Burns.
evidence.quote: In 1881, Charles Fields established a homestead where the community of Fields is located today.  Fields built a stagecoach roadhouse to serve the stage route between Winnemucca, Nevada, and Burns.

evidence.claim: He sold the business to John Smyth in 1911; the post office followed two years later.
evidence.quote: Fields sold his business to John Smyth in 1911.  The Fields post office was opened two years later.

evidence.claim: The stone roadhouse was remodeled into a store and restaurant and remains in use.
evidence.quote: The stone roadhouse was eventually remodeled into a store and restaurant, and is still in use.

evidence.claim: The surrounding ranches use Fields as a center of commerce.
evidence.quote: It is the center of commerce for local ranches

evidence.claim: A school, campground and a few houses are part of the community at the tour’s end.
evidence.quote: Today, the community of Fields consists of a bar, store, cafe, gas station, school, campground, and a few houses.

evidence.claim: Ranching in the Fields area began in 1869 with the establishment of Whitehorse Ranch.
evidence.quote: Ranching began in the area in 1869 when Whitehorse Ranch was established.

evidence.claim: Steens rises a vertical mile from the Alvord Basin to nearly 10,000 feet, giving the road a mountain face on one side of the desert.
evidence.quote: It is the largest fault-block mountain in the northern Great Basin, rising a vertical mile from the Alvord Basin to an elevation of nearly 10,000 feet.

evidence.claim: About 13,000 years ago, the larger lake breached Big Sand Gap, sending several cubic miles of water into the Coyote Lake basin.
evidence.quote: About 13,000 years ago, the lake breached Big Sand Gap and sent several cubic miles of water into the Coyote Lake basin.

evidence.claim: A one-room school was established around 1900, with a single teacher.
evidence.quote: A one-room school was established at the site around 1900 with one teacher.

flags: The cache calls this an Oregon Tour Route, not a National Scenic Byway; used that specific identity.
ODOT gives 143 miles; material maps 129.3. Used the official tour length without conflating it with mapped mileage.
No construction or campaigning history for the entire tour is cached. History is limited to Route 78 numbering and George Renwick’s attributed account of earlier playa travel.
ODOT calls Alvord Hot Springs no-fee; the Alvord cache says charging began in 2013. Omitted hot-springs access and fee claims.
No current story claims were dropped for lack of evidence. No story-level motifs were present in current; supplied an empty array.
Fields remains a town moment about its stage-route origins and ranching role, not a business recommendation.
